lead: Closed-loop frequency response tells how the finished feedback system responds to sine waves, but solving T(jω)=G(jω)/(1+G(jω)) at every frequency is slow. M and N circles draw constant closed-loop magnitude and phase directly in the open-loop plane. The Nichols chart moves the same contours to a gain-in-dB versus phase-in-degrees grid, where an open-loop frequency curve can be plotted point by point. Engineers use these charts to read resonant peak, resonant frequency and bandwidth without factoring the characteristic equation. Unity feedback is assumed here.
prereq: You need: 4.1 Frequency response, 4.3 Bode plots, 4.5 Nyquist plot, 4.6 Gain and phase margins, and complex arithmetic.

sections.h3: From open-loop G to closed-loop T

blocks.text: With unity feedback, the closed-loop transfer function is T(s)=G(s)/(1+G(s)). Put s=jω. Write G(jω)=X+jY, where X is the real part and Y is the imaginary part. The closed-loop magnitude is M=|T(jω)|. The closed-loop phase is φ=∠T(jω). M is a pure number; φ is in degrees or radians.

blocks.where: G(jω) is the open-loop frequency response; T(jω) is the closed-loop frequency response for unity feedback.

blocks.text: The characteristic equation is 1+G(s)=0. Near a frequency where G(jω) approaches −1, the denominator is small and M becomes large. That is why the point −1 controls both stability and resonance. Solving T at every ω means complex division at every frequency. The M and N circles avoid this: they are fixed contours drawn once in the G-plane. Any computed G(jω) point falls on one M contour and one N contour, so closed-loop magnitude and phase are read directly. The Nichols chart applies the same idea with different axes.

Set M=|T|. From M²=|G|²/|1+G|² one obtains the M-circle equation. For M≠1 it is a circle in the X-Y plane. Every point on it gives closed-loop magnitude M. For M=2 the centre is (−4/3,0) and the radius is 2/3. For M=4 the centre is (−16/15,0) and the radius is 4/15. Larger M gives a smaller circle closer to −1+j0.

blocks.where: X=Re G(jω), Y=Im G(jω), M=|T(jω)|. Centre is (−M²/(M²−1), 0); radius is M/|M²−1|. Valid for M≠1.

blocks.text: For M=1 the denominator M²−1 is zero. The equation reduces to 2X+1=0, that is X=−1/2. This is a vertical straight line, not a circle.

The phase contours use N=tan φ, where φ=∠T. For G=X+jY, completing squares gives the N-circle equation. Each N circle is the locus of constant N=tan φ, that is constant closed-loop phase modulo 180°. One contour serves φ and φ+180°; the chart labels distinguish the actual phase branch.

blocks.where: N=tan φ; φ=∠T(jω). Centre is (−1/2, 1/(2N)); radius is √(1/4 + 1/(4N²)).

sections.h3: Nichols chart and reading closed-loop values

blocks.text: The Nichols chart plots open-loop gain 20log10|G(jω)| in dB on the vertical axis and open-loop phase ∠G(jω) in degrees on the horizontal axis. The M and N circles of the G-plane are redrawn as M and N contours on this grid. A point on an M contour has the same closed-loop magnitude M.

items: Choose frequencies ω1, ω2, ... covering the range of interest.
Convert to gain 20log10√(X²+Y²) dB and phase atan2(Y,X) degrees.
Plot each pair (phase, gain) and join the points in increasing ω.
At each point, read the surrounding M and N contours.
The largest M on the curve is the resonant peak Mr; the frequency there is ωr. The bandwidth ωb is the frequency where M falls to |T(0)|/√2, that is 3 dB below the low-frequency closed-loop gain.

blocks.text: Changing gain K shifts the curve vertically on a Nichols chart. The shape stays the same and the M readings change. This is how gain adjustment is judged on the chart.

figure.caption: Constant-M circles in the open-loop plane. The G(j2) point lies inside the M=2 circle and outside the M=4 circle, so 2<M<4.

spec.aria: Constant-M circles for M=2 and M=4 in the open-loop plane; the point for G(j2) lies inside the M=2 circle and just outside the M=4 circle.

examples.question: For a unity-feedback system G(s)=50/[s(s+1)(s+10)], evaluate G(j2). Then find the closed-loop T(j2), its magnitude M in dB and closed-loop phase φ in degrees; also compute N=tan φ. State whether the point lies inside the M=2 circle or the M=4 circle.
steps: At ω=2 rad/s, s=j2. (1+j2)(10+j2)=6+j22. Multiplying by j2 gives j2(6+j22)=−44+j12. Hence G(j2)=50/(−44+j12).

M=2 circle: centre (−1.333,0), radius 0.667. Distance from G(j2) to centre = √[(−1.058+1.333)²+(−0.289)²]=0.399<0.667, so inside. M=4 circle: centre (−1.067,0), radius 0.267. Distance = √[(−1.058+1.067)²+(−0.289)²]=0.289>0.267, so outside. Thus 2<M<4.
examples.answer: T(j2)=1.667−j3.333, M=3.727 (11.43 dB), φ=−63.435°, N=tan φ=−2.000; the point is inside the M=2 circle and outside the M=4 circle.
examples.check:
import cmath, math
s = 1j*2
G = 50/(s*(s+1)*(s+10))
T = G/(1+G)
M = abs(T)
phi = math.degrees(cmath.phase(T))
N = math.tan(math.radians(phi))
dB = 20*math.log10(M)
print(f"{M:.5f}")
print(f"{phi:.5f}")
print(f"{dB:.5f}")
print(f"{N:.5f}")

traps: M circles live in the open-loop G-plane, not the closed-loop plane.
The critical point is −1. A point on the M=1 line has closed-loop magnitude 1, not open-loop magnitude 1.
Nichols chart axes are open-loop gain in dB and open-loop phase in degrees; do not plot closed-loop phase on the horizontal axis.
On an N circle, N is tan φ, not φ itself.
Bandwidth is read from closed-loop magnitude, not from the −3 dB point of the open-loop Bode gain.

quiz.q: State the two axes of a Nichols chart.
quiz.a: Vertical axis: open-loop gain 20log10|G(jω)| in dB. Horizontal axis: open-loop phase ∠G(jω) in degrees.

quiz.q: What is the M=1 locus in the G-plane?
Why are M circles drawn in the open-loop plane rather than the closed-loop plane?
quiz.a: The open-loop G(jω) is known or measured. T is then obtained from T=G/(1+G). Drawing M circles in the G-plane lets us read |T| directly from the known G point without computing T at every frequency.

quiz.q: A point has G=−1+j0.6. Is it inside the M=2 circle?
quiz.a: M=2 circle: centre (−1.333,0), radius 0.667. Distance from (−1,0.6) to centre is √(0.333²+0.6²)=0.686. This is greater than 0.667, so the point is outside the M=2 circle.

quiz.q: On a Nichols chart, an open-loop point has gain 6 dB and phase −120°. The M contour through it reads 1.4. If this is the highest M on the curve, find Mr and state whether a resonant peak exists.
quiz.a: Mr=1.4. A resonant peak exists because Mr>1.

quiz.q: Explain why increasing open-loop gain shifts a Nichols curve upward and can increase Mr.
quiz.a: Adding gain adds a constant dB to every point, so the whole curve moves up. In the G-plane this moves the curve closer to −1. The curve can enter higher-M contours, so the largest M on the curve, Mr, rises. Too much gain makes the curve pass near or around −1 and the system becomes unstable.

quiz.q: A G(jω) curve lies entirely outside the M=2 circle. Can the closed-loop system have Mr=2.5? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Outside the M=2 circle in that region, closed-loop magnitude is less than 2. If the whole curve stays outside, every point has M<2, so Mr<2. Mr=2.5 would require some part of the curve to lie inside the M=2 circle.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Nichols charts are built into control software and are used when a plant model is known but a full closed-loop simulation is expensive. Modern robust control uses singular-value plots for multivariable systems, which generalize M circles. Search for “Nichols chart MATLAB”, “M circle closed-loop frequency response”, and “sigma plot robust control”.
